newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thailand in dilemma over rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thailand in dilemma over rate cuts.

text.p: Thailand is in a dilemma over what to do about current high interest rates and their negative impact on businesses and the flagging economy.
The economy is unlikely to bounce back quickly after the marginal 25 basis points reductions in lending rates made recently by major Thai banks, analysts said.
Current sluggish consumption, stifled business activity and weak investments will only be given a shot in the arm if much deeper cuts in the rates are made soon, they told Reuters.

"The 25 basis points (reductions made last week) is nothing and not going to help the economy. The economy needs at least 200-300 basis points cuts in interest rates," said Jimmy Koh, an economist at Singapore-based I.D.E.A.
Several leading Thai banks last week reduced their deposit and lending rates following repeated calls by the business community for cheaper funds to uplift the slowing economy.
Thai lending rates at around 12.75-13.00 are among the highest in the region. They have sparked a liquidity crunch that has hit the troubled finance and property sectors hard.
The Bank of Thailand remains cautious about sharper reductions in rates although Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan is pushing hard for deeper cuts.
The central bank keeps rates high to attract capital inflows and to fight off speculative attacks on the baht.
The baht came under attack in mid-May from players goaded by the slumping economic picture.
Private analysts say Thailand's economic growth this year may fall to three to five percent compared with the latest official projections of 5.9 percent and versus 6.4 percent in 1996.
Other economic woes gripping Thailand are a sharp slowdown in exports growth and a plunging stock market hovering near eight year lows.
But prospects for deeper rate cuts look dim.
"The high rates have to be maintained in order to defend the baht from any future speculative attacks," the Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand said in a latest report.
Analysts said if rates were lowered, inflows of foreign funds to finance the high current account deficit could be hit.
Thailand's current account deficit is seen officially at about six percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year compared with 8.2 percent in 1996.

"At this moment, the economy is still reliant on offshore inflows. If Thailand does cut interest rates too much, that could create instability in the financial system," said Andy Tan, general manager at MMS International in Singapore.
The central bank hit foreign baht speculators hard last month when it cut off their short-term baht supply by telling Thai banks not to lend baht to them or to make rates highly prohibitive.
This move could also cut off some of the much-needed foreign inflows, analysts said.

"You must understand that whenever foreign funds come into Thailand, they actually need the hedging facilities available in the forward market. Right now there is no liquidity in the forward market (after the central bank's move," said Koh.

By cutting off the baht supply to foreign players after the latest speculative attack, the central bank informally created a two-tier exchange rate system with one rate being quoted offshore and another onshore.

"Currency speculators will no doubt continue to test the central bank's resolve frequently," said Capital Nomura Securities in a new report. "Consequently, unless the Bank of Thailand changes its stance against maintaining its current inflexible exchange rate system, there appears little scope for a further decline in short term interest rates."
